I mentioned in another post that I was adapting the Elo rating system for use with the MLB. The TL;DR of it is 1500 is average, higher is better, and lower is worse. I've written a program to track the ratings, and am using Nate Silver's old methodology except for my handling of the offseason: instead of returning each team's rating halfway to 1500 after each season, I instead back-generated a rating using the average of each team's record projection as published by PECOTA and BaseRuns. So, here are the ratings after 10-ish games:

*How well a team is currently playing; that is, their expected 2015 record if the season started today

**Team's expected 2015 record given their current record and Elo rating

The first thing that might jump out at you is the tightness of the grouping; it only goes from 1561 to 1439. This is because in baseball, unlike other major sports, even the worst team in the league can expect to win at least 50 or 60 games out of 162, and even the best team can expect to lose as many. Thus the amount of skill from top to bottom doesn't vary that much, and the bunching reflects that. Some teams' ratings might be surprising given their records. There are two reasons for these cases: (1) Only ten games have been recorded, so most teams have not yet had sufficient chance to deviate from their preseason projections too much, and (2) much more goes into the ratings than simple record. As mentioned, margin of victory, strength of schedule, and other factors are at play. Teams' rating velocity is small by design; each game usually only moves team ratings by somewhere between 2–4 points (although there are always games outside that range).

On to the analysis: as you can see, the top and bottom three teams remain the same from the afternoon of April 5th, but that's about it. Washington, after beginning the season 2–6 and falling to 1534.99, recovered 7.80 points and hold a 2.87 point buffer to retain the 2 spot. St. Louis has begun the season 2 wins better than expected to hold a comfortable lead in third, while the Dodgers have increased their lead (which was respectable to begin with) by 11.20. They are the obvious leader, and are expected to finish with 95 wins, 6 better than Washington. Meanwhile, at the other end, Atlanta has faded from their 5–0 start, peaking at 1478.38 and settling down to 1473.51. The Twins and the Phillies, rounding out the bottom, are trying to win the first 2016 draft pick early; Minnesota has faded from a 90-loss team to a 93-loss team after ten games, while Philadelphia has gone from 93 losses to 97. Minnesota’s case may be surprising, given their 4–6 record; however, they already have losses by 11-, 6-, 4-, and 9-run margins to mostly middling teams, while squeezing out wins by 1, 3, 2, and 6 runs (the last coming against the #26 White Sox, who won the series).

The good The biggest positive surprises in the field have been Kansas City (who started 7–0 after being projected to win 75), the Rockies (who won their first game 10–0 in a stadium not named Coors Field), and the New York Baseball Mets, who have not lost since April 11. Detroit, who began the season projected to win 83 games, sports the best record in baseball at 9–1 (their lone loss being a one-run near-comeback at Pittsburgh) and have the biggest Elo jump so far, picking up 22.2 points and a projected 8 extra wins.

Baltimore, whose fans were just a wee bit vocal after their mediocre preseason projections, has started the season 5–5 and are exactly on pace to meet their projections.

The bad The biggest tank so far (in terms of position) is Milwaukee, who have the worst record so far at 2–8 including a home sweep by Colorado (with a cumulative series score of 20–6) to begin the season. Miami, tied with Philadelphia to floor the NL East, has lost five games from their preseason .500 projection.

The ugly San Francisco, realizing 2015 is not an even-numbered year, have promptly begun the season 3–9 and have not won a game since their 1–0 win at San Diego. MadBum, for his part, has a pedestrian 1.41 WHIP and wears an ERA well over 5.0.

Coming up: Washington, in the middle of the biggest point-disparity series of the next 10 game period, will follow up immediately with the combined highest-point matchup over the same period. They currently have 129.19 points on the Phillies (25 points are added for home field advantage for calculating win expectancy). This means that they would be expected to win 67.78% of the games in the series (moneyline: -210). They will then have a 54.0% win expectancy (-117 moneyline) when St. Louis comes to visit Tuesday through Thursday. As this is the highest-rated matchup in the next week and a half, this should be the best baseball played over the period, so if you can only watch one series besides your own teams', that's the one to watch.

This is the first of what will be a recurring Elo report series every ten games or so; I'll bring in a few more and different stats as more games are played. I've written a program to keep track of all of this (it even generated the above table), so if anyone has any specific questions or curiosities about matchups, let me know and I'll probably have an answer for you. Also let me know if you have suggestions for future posts!
